title: Creation Changes; the Spirit Is Unchangeable and Eternal
english: … thing it is corrupted, so that on this account it loses, as it were, its title to be called eternal. For anything whatever that goes out of itself, that is, is altered, meets death, even if it lasts on in some other way: its own alteration is that death. Whatever you may conceive as having come to be afterwards is the death of what was there before. So, for instance, when wickedness turns into goodness, it is put to death by the goodness in the one from whom it has departed; and conversely, goodness is put to death by wickedness. For there are some beings that will not bear to stand always in their first station, although this was never denied them.

So it is that Peter and Jude state this plainly in their letters. Peter: “For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into Tartarus in chains of gloom and has kept them for the judgment of the great day, and did not spare the ancient world …” (2 Peter 2:4-5). And Jude: “And the angels who did not keep their own original rank, but abandoned their proper dwelling, he has kept under gloom in everlasting bonds for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).

The bodily rational creation admits alteration. It is altered in disposition, as when Judas lost his sanctification, and as Paul writes: “But the widow who lives for pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6), though she is still living out her life among men. And it is altered in substance, when it first comes to an end and then passes over into immortality. “For this corruptible,” he says, “must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53).

The non-rational creation undergoes turning and passes away. So, when the light was turning into darkness and the water into blood, it was prophesied: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” And elsewhere: “Heaven,” he says, “and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35). For it was prophesied that there will be new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). And this is true: everything that has received a beginning also has an end.

But the Holy Spirit is of the ineffable nature that rules over all things, eternal and incorruptible. He is always the same and in the same respects. He alone knows and does the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:11). He guards all things: the rational beings who are perfect in faith, and the non-rational too, until the term given to the non-rational for their continuance in sameness. So by nature and by will he stands incapable of turning and change; that is, he is incorruptible. What cannot turn, that is, what is incorruptible, is at once without beginning, without end and above the ages; and what is without beginning is the Maker, not a thing made. That is why Wisdom says with full propriety: “Your incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1); and Peter: “in the incorruptibility of the gentle and quiet spirit” (1 Peter 3:4).

So too the Father, who is always equal to himself and like himself, admitting neither slackening toward the worse nor heightening toward the better, is spoken of by James as the one “with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning” (James 1:17), and by Paul as “the incorruptible, invisible, only wise God” (1 Timothy 1:17). In the same way the Son too was attested in the hundred and second Psalm: “But you, Lord, remain for ever” (Psalm 102:12); and again: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed; but you are the same always, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:25-27; Hebrews 1:10-12).
That he is eternal.

Creation does not possess eternity once for all and in its own right. First, because it does not have it of itself: it obtained it for the time to come, from the moment it came to be, as a gift shared by the God who alone, and above the ages, exists of himself. For being good he creates, and in the end, presiding over his own work, he generously bestows eternity on it. Secondly, for the reasons explained in the chapter before this one.

But the Holy Spirit has eternity by nature, as befitted the creating and good Spirit of God, who works all things eternally, is never himself bounded, and yet can set bounds to the things made by him; and so he was honoured with this title. You may learn this, if you will follow me, in the following way. Paul writes to the Hebrews: “who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God” (Hebrews 9:14). He means Christ the Master, who in his holy incarnation offered himself through the Holy Spirit to his own Father in our place. Peter too sounds the same note, as was already mentioned: “But the word of God remains for ever” (1 Peter 1:25). For here he calls the Spirit of God “word of God”. Indeed, because the Godhead of the Father and of the Son is the same, Paul, when he mentions them, uses the same reverent expression: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “knows, he who is blessed for ever” (2 Corinthians 11:31); and again: “Jesus Christ yesterday and …

title: The Heretics’ Argument on “Eternal” Answered
english: … today, the same for ever” (Hebrews 13:8). But what those who are hostile to the theology of the Holy Spirit have laid down on this head too cannot, simply cannot, be borne by the ear. For prejudice carries them off to the ends of the earth, and an undiscerning passion does not usually show the marks of careful examination. Still, nothing hinders us, so to speak, from hearing that very piece of plausible pleading; for in this way they would be condemned all the more.

It runs like this. If something has been called “eternal” by a shared name, it cannot for that reason be called God; rather, if anyone is God, he is the maker of eternal things. For it is written: “God is the maker of times and ages”; and again: “In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old in the prophets; in the last of the days he has spoken to us in a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebrews 1:1-2). For if a thing has been called eternal, it is not bound to be named God; otherwise there will be countless gods. For it is written: “And be lifted up, eternal gates” (Psalm 24:7); and again: “Eternal years were remembered” (Psalm 77:5); and once more: “like eternal sheep”; and: “These will rise to eternal punishment” (Matthew 25:46); and elsewhere: “Those in the dust of the earth will rise, some to eternal life, and some to eternal shame” (Daniel 12:2). Are the punishment and the shame gods, then? You see into how much absurdity and impiety this sharing of the name “eternal” falls.

Now in their thoughts and words a brine floats on the surface and is mixed all through; but what follows dissolves it. As we mentioned just now, the other things, even if they did obtain the name “eternal”, not only obtained it from a point in time, but are also subject to corruption, the turning that comes from their own will; and their “eternal” is altogether unlike the divine eternal. In the same way, one who is called holy, whether angel or man, is not holy in like and equal measure with the Spirit, the holy of holies; for the Spirit is holiness and eternity entire.

Let them attend, then, to the grandeur of speech with which “eternal” has been proclaimed of the Holy Spirit, and to the fact that Paul added to it that wonderful thing, beyond the grasp of all: I mean that through the Holy Spirit the one who fashioned the ages offered himself to his own true Father on our behalf. Let them consider, too, that all the powers of the heavens are in the Holy Spirit, surely as in the fellow-creator of the Creator who needs nothing; and that the very oracles we brought forward on this head foretold the end of those eternal gates and sheep which the heretics mentioned, not to the point but for effect.

And let the difference be clear to them between what is eternal without beginning and without change, and what is eternal from a point in time and is changeable. Let it be clear that this difference is not small, nor does it lie only in the substance and in some further beauty: it is a difference in every respect. Let this too be known: the Holy Spirit, when called eternal, is to be judged alongside God the Father, who gave strength to all things, and alongside the Son, not alongside the creatures. So let them give up the worse opinion and choose the better. Instead of what they admire now, let them admire what is worth admiring, and let them fare better in the time to come; no one grudges it. And from the very points on which they hurt themselves by their boastful fault-finding, let them now carry off the profit of repentance.

For if this word was used of God the Father and of the Son as showing something worthy of God, it would be taken equally and in the same way of the Spirit of God. That is one point. Another is this: none of the “eternal” things they mentioned has been called divine, or Holy Spirit proceeding from God, or even a single being rather than a multitude. None is ranked with the Father and the Son in the divine initiation and the divine gift; nor, not to say more, has any been thought worthy of any other honour that belongs to the Godhead.

There are other points besides. God the Father was pleased that all things should be created through his Son, the Word. And what slur, as they dream, is it on his all-holy Spirit that he did not create, unless indeed, by their account, he is not ineffably a co-worker with the Creator, as the Father is? That every working and gift, creative, good and perfect, belongs to his only-begotten Son the Word and to the one Holy Spirit and is common to them, while all of it is referred back to the One from whom and with whom these blessed hypostases shone forth in a way past telling: this anyone would learn very easily who quietly examined the oracles full of wisdom, both those cited in various places of this book and those in the book before it. And Paul too, greater than human measure, set this out, affirming it plainly to the Corinthians: “But you were washed, but you were justified, but …

title: The Spirit Re-creates, Admits No Change, and Is Holy by Nature
english: … you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Observe, then, observe: if the name of the Son is a divine name, as indeed it is, then beyond all doubt so is the name of the Holy Spirit; for he made plain one name belonging to both. Observe too that the Holy Spirit, as he ineffably shared in creating at the beginning, now also creates anew; for “to be washed” signified “to be created anew”. And to Titus he writes: “having begotten us again through the washing of rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). The sacred psalmist, no less, would have us know that those who already exist by birth are now being created spiritually in the divine font. For he says: “A people that is being created will praise the Lord” (Psalm 102:18).

So, then, the hypostases that have the same honour and the same working have received the same nature as their portion. They differ from one another in nothing, in Godhead or in power, and they alone can be naturally joined with the One, ranked with him, and everywhere conceived together with him. He it is who has both from himself, without beginning, on equal and like terms, united with him and bound to him in a way past speaking, though he himself is not the hypostases of the two.

Further, besides what has been said: every plea of these heretics follows the same pattern, and uses the same words, as the stale sophistry of theirs that is now in motion; we shall learn this by experience before long from the chapters themselves. For if some word, say “eternal” or “good”, which carries a divine meaning about the Trinity in unity and belongs to it wholly and perfectly, happens to have been said somewhere of a creature, with the qualification proper to a creature, they say nothing about God the Father and his Son (what indeed could they say?); but at once, most senselessly, they bring the Holy Spirit down to the creation, instead of raising him, as is most fitting, to God and the Only-begotten, whom the theologians have most aptly praised in like and equal terms with the Holy Spirit.

Now the arguments we have put forward in the chapter we are pursuing cannot, even on their own, be got past, and they suffice for the whole contest with the heretics. So either let them show (a thing very grievous even to say) that a beginning or an end of the Holy Spirit has been declared anywhere in the oracles; or that he had any road at all toward corruption, as angelic and human choice has; or else, as the saying goes, let “an ox stand on their tongue”. So much for them. I shall now pass on to the subject I set out from.
That, being unchangeable, he admits neither virtue nor vice.

The rational creation admits both virtue and vice. Among the bodiless, as we said before, we find the approved angels within virtue and those cast out within vice; and so too among beings in bodies, such as we ourselves are. But the divine Spirit is above virtue and glory, or rather is himself the spring from which the highest virtue flows, and he admits none of these, as neither does the Father nor the Son. If he does not admit them, neither is his will other than theirs; and if that is so (for he does all that the Father wills), neither is his substance other. From this, then, two things are gathered: that he is not a creature, but stands toward God the Father and his Son without any difference; and that through him we know that God, from whom he proceeded by nature, is in us too, as it is written (1 John 3:24).
That he is holy by nature, and sanctifies and justifies.

Creation is sanctified and justified by God, who is holy by nature; for it is able to receive sanctification and justification, not to bestow them. But the Holy Spirit stands apart from creation and is joined by nature to him from whom he has proceeded, the one about whom we were taught in the mysteries that “every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning” (James 1:17). He cares and provides for all, even for the guilty. So he sanctifies, justifies and makes wise, and furnishes every form of heavenly virtue; but he himself is in no way found to have any capacity to be sanctified, justified or made wise by another, just as neither has the self-existent Father nor his Son, who shares his nature. For this reason too he is rightly praised as holy in himself and as “Spirit of holiness” (Romans 1:4), that is, holy by nature and of himself; as “divine Spirit”, that is, God by nature; and as “breath of the Almighty” (Job 33:4), that is, consubstantial with the Almighty, breathed forth from his hypostasis. Even one such name, then, taken alone, shows him to be consubstantial with God the Father, and sanctifying, and beyond the reach even of reason. Accordingly Paul, mighty both to speak and to set out the patterns of the faith, …
